title: Tazria: the skin affliction (Leviticus 13)
hook: not leprosy as we know it; the rabbis linked it to harmful speech

segments.voice: Yesterday, after a birth: a mother's time apart, and an offering anyone could afford. Your line was birth changes everything. Today, a chapter that's hard to love.

Leviticus thirteen is fifty-nine verses of rashes: white spots, raw flesh, hair turning yellow, patches that spread or don't. It's an easy chapter to skim. Older English Bibles called the condition leprosy, and that word carries centuries of fear. But read closely and something doesn't fit. The same affliction can appear on a wool garment, a leather bag, and later on the stone walls of a house. Whatever this is, it isn't the disease called leprosy today. So what is it?
screen: `FIFTY-NINE VERSES OF RASHES.` → `ON CLOTHES. ON WALLS.` → `SO WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the name. The Hebrew is tzara'at. When the Torah was translated into Greek, the word used was lepra, and from there English got leprosy. But Hansen's disease, what's called leprosy now, doesn't grow on fabric or walls. There may be no exact modern match, and Maimonides wrote that tzara'at was not a natural illness at all but a sign. The Talmud plays on the word for the afflicted person, metzora, and hears motzi shem ra: one who spreads a bad name. In this reading, tzara'at is what harmful speech looks like when it finally shows. There's a story behind it. In the book of Numbers, Miriam speaks against her brother Moses, and she is struck with tzara'at, white as snow. Aaron pleads with Moses for her, Moses prays, and the whole camp waits seven days for her to return. Later, Deuteronomy tells the people to remember what was done to Miriam on the way out of Egypt. The rabbis heard that as: remember what words can do. Maimonides, following an older midrash, adds an order. The affliction starts on the walls of the house, then the clothes, and only then the skin: a warning, a closer warning, then the body. Words work the same way, a remark at the edges of a group, then closer, until it sits on someone's skin. Jewish law has a name for harmful true speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, and whole books on avoiding it.
screen: `NOT THE LEPROSY WE KNOW.` · `METZORA: ONE WHO SPREADS A BAD NAME.` · `MIRIAM, WHITE AS SNOW.` · `WALLS, CLOTHES, THEN SKIN.` · then, large: `WORDS SHOW ON THE SKIN.`

segments.voice: Think back over yesterday's conversations, the texts, the group chats, the comment in the kitchen, and look for a sentence about someone who wasn't there. True or not, notice how it felt to say it, and how it would feel to hear it about yourself. Then bring to mind one person you'd like to speak of only kindly, or not at all.
Tzara'at. The skin affliction of Leviticus, not the leprosy we know, which the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible.
Your line: words show on the skin. What's said about others leaves a mark. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Jews study the laws of lashon hara, harmful speech, especially from the Chafetz Chaim's books, and some keep a daily study schedule on guarding the tongue; the portions Tazria and Metzora are often taught as lessons about speech.

original.note: Hebrew: the skin affliction of Leviticus 13–14; translated into Greek as lepra, and so into English as leprosy.

trapdoor: what it means: a ritual affliction of skin, cloth and walls, which the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible.
what a scholar hears: the Septuagint's lepra meant scaly skin, not Hansen's disease; Arakhin 15b–16a ties tzara'at to lashon hara, and Maimonides calls it a sign, not a natural illness.

chat.says: Isn't tzara'at in the Bible just leprosy?
options: Probably not: it shows up on clothes and walls, and the rabbis read it as harmful speech.
Yes, and the rabbis read it as a punishment for eating food that wasn't kosher.
It's a sign of holiness, so the priest marked those who had it as future leaders.
